      Texas jet plant


      A lean final assembly plant for a midsize business jet. The line moves at takt, the cells build to kanban, andon stops the line. Change the plan and watch it run.

      How this plant is designed

      The jet is our own midsize twin (24 m long, 23 m span, aft engines, T tail), not a real type. The plant is designed from a demand target: takt is the available shift time in a month divided by the jets the customers want. At 6 a month on two shifts that is 56 shift hours, 3.5 working days, and the moving line advances one 36 m station in that time, about 0.4 inches a minute.

      The final assembly work (4,370 labour hours in 22 tasks, our own estimate) is balanced over the stations so the busiest carries as little as possible, and each crew is sized to finish in 88 % of the cycle. Upstream the wing and fuselage cells build to kanban, two sets of cards each; engines and interiors are bought on cards sized by demand times lead time. Paint has two bays, the flight line five stands.

      The model is a discrete event simulation: it moves straight from one event to the next (a task done, a jet at the end of a station, a machine down or repaired, a kit done, a truck in, a shift change). Task times vary (log normal, 12 % spread, 3 % rework); machines fail at random. Automated checks: the line reaches a steady state, meets demand, keeps WIP flat, obeys Little's law, does not overproduce, and falls short in the cases it should.

      The machines and their physics

      The equipment is modelled after the real thing and moves by its own physics. The fuselage cell's robots are KUKA KR 500 class arms on linear tracks with a multi function end effector; every hole is reached by inverse kinematics inside the joint limits, and the one pass cycle (clamp, drill and countersink, probe, sealant, insert, release) takes 7.1 s, about 8.5 fasteners a minute. The wing cell's C frame riveters follow Electroimpact's wing panel machines at 12 slug rivets a minute. The 20 t bridge cranes run at the two speed figures of a 28 m span Hak crane (bridge 15/60 m/min, trolley 7.5/30, hoist 2.4/12) with acceleration limits, and the load swings on the ropes as a pendulum when the bridge starts and stops. Fuselage and wing joins are aligned with Leica AT960 class laser trackers (15 µm + 6 µm/m): the positioners move by most of what was measured, the trackers shoot again, until the residual reads inside 0.25 mm; the rounds and minutes it takes are random, as they are on the floor, and are charged to the station. Crews ride a 97 % learning curve. The test flight's takeoff roll is integrated from thrust, weight, lift and drag for a Praetor 600 class jet (two 33.5 kN engines, 21.5 m span) and lands within the published field length.

      Lean, from the airsup lean notes

      Take the buffers out so problems surface; pull instead of push; stabilise and standardise before levelling; make the state of the work visible from across the room (andon boards at every station, the plant board at the head of the line); put parts at the point of use (flow racks, supermarkets beside the stations that use them); automate the constraint, not the loudest problem.

      Real lines this follows

      
        Boeing 737, Renton: moving line at 2 inches a minute, flow time cut from 22 to 11 days, five jets on the line against about two dozen in work before. Boeing, Assembly

        Boeing 737 panel assembly line: automated machines fasten stringers to wing skins at twice the old rate. AIN

        Airbus A321XLR final assembly, Hamburg: station sequence from monuments and fuselage join (over 3,000 rivets) to wing join (about 2,400 rivets a wing), power on, tests. Airbus

        Embraer Melbourne: Phenom line with its own paint shop, up to 8 jets a month at full capacity. Airframer

        Business jet deliveries, 854 in 2025. GAMA

        Renton paint hangar: about 3 days a 737. Boeing

        Airbus Hamburg fuselage structure line: 20 robots, 1,100 to 2,400 holes a longitudinal joint, 3,000 rivets at the orbital joint, AGVs and laser positioning. AIN

      
      The equipment

      
        Electroimpact wing panel riveters: E4320 at Broughton 12 slug rivets or 8 lockbolts a minute, E6000 16 a minute, E7000 fuselage 20 a minute. Electroimpact, E6000

        Robotic one pass fastening with a multi function end effector (clamp, drill and countersink, inspect, sealant, insert) on KUKA class robots. Electroimpact, SAE 2017-01-2094, KUKA

        Broetje multi panel assembly cell: 10 axis positioner, all electric end effector, flexible tooling to ±0.1 mm. Broetje

        Leica Absolute Tracker AT960: 3D measuring volume to 40 m, 6DoF to 20 m. Hexagon

        20 t double girder bridge crane, 28 m span: hoist 2.4/12, trolley 7.5/30, bridge 15/60 m/min. Hak

        Air bearing and omnidirectional transporters under fuselages and wings, millimetre positioning. Assembly, HUBTEX

        Praetor 600: 21.5 m span, 20.74 m long, MTOW 19,440 kg, two Honeywell HTF7500E of 7,528 lbf, takeoff 4,717 ft at MTOW, sea level, ISA. Jetcraft, AOPA

      
      Simplified: labour hours, crews, hand fastening rates, mean time between failures and lead times are our own scenario numbers; the robots drill a representative sample of their holes on screen; transporter speeds are assumed (vendors publish capacity, not speed); weekends are left out; only the takeoff roll is flown by a flight model, the rest of the sortie is scripted; no certification, cost or supplier risk. A design study, not a real plant.
